card.hook: You don't need to be clever here, because the colours do the work for you: cobalt-blue walls, red trim, green barred windows and a big tree hanging over the street. Just don't be surprised if about 25,000 other people a month had the same idea.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Londres and Allende, with the house about 30 m to the north, so face north. From this corner you get the whole blue corner facade in one frame, showing two walls at once.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full corner. If the pavement is narrow or you want the tree and sky in too, tap 0.5x. Use 2x for a closer shot of the windows and trim without stepping into the road.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the blue wall, then slide it a touch darker so the blue stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, roughly 3:30 to 5:00 pm, should give side light on the facade, but check it on the day. Weekday mornings are calmer for crowds, though the entrance side may be in shade.
card.selfie_here: Inside the courtyard garden, turn to the front camera and stand with the blue walls and greenery behind you, though you'll probably share the view with other visitors. Another classic is posing beside the sign that says Frida and Diego lived in this house. Sources don't say exactly where it is, so keep an eye out when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to stand on the pavement at the Londres and Allende corner, stepping back until the blue corner facade and the tree fill the frame, while you pose in front of the house.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside can be photographed from the public street, but the museum is ticketed and has its own photo rules, so check the official site before you go. Inside, selfie sticks go in the cloakroom with your bag, flash and video are not allowed, and photos without flash are OK in the patios and gardens.
card.challenge: Get the red trim, the green barred windows and the blue wall all in one frame, then see if you can sneak the tree in at the top too.
card.good_to_know: La Casa Azul is where Frida Kahlo was born, grew up and later died. It was built in 1904 and has since been simplified to the plainer facade you see today. Diego Rivera gave the house and its contents to be turned into a museum in her honour, and it has been open as one since 1958.

card.hook: Picture nine giant letters, a spiky maguey plant and a mariachi band tuning up right behind them. That's the Plaza Garibaldi postcard, and you can get it in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in front of Mercado San Camilito, beside the big GARIBALDI letters. The middle of the square is to the south of this spot, about 2 minutes on foot, so face south and let the letters, the maguey and the musicians fall into one view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the letters with the performers behind. If you're close to the letters, tap zoom 0.5x to fit the whole sign and the market front in. Use zoom 2x, if your phone has it, for musicians farther away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the letters up with a horizontal line so they sit level, and don't cut off the end letters.
card.best_time: The square is liveliest in the evening, and Friday or Saturday night from 11:00 p.m. is a good choice for the full atmosphere. Want fewer people in front of the letters? Come in daylight.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the giant GARIBALDI letters, on the side facing the market, which one guide calls an Instagram hotspot. Use the front camera (or zoom 0.5x on the back one), and keep the letters over your shoulder so the mariachis and dancers fill the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before taking close-ups of mariachi bands. If you ask a band to pose, agree on a tip first (one guide suggests 50-100 MXN). The streets around the plaza can feel less safe at night, so stay on the main plaza in well-lit areas and keep your phone and bag close.
card.challenge: Can you get all nine letters level in the frame, with a musician mid-strum behind them and no cut-off letters?
card.good_to_know: The plaza was called Plaza Santa Cecilia until 1920, when it was renamed after Lt. Col. Peppino Garibaldi, who fought in the Mexican Revolution. Mariachi players have gathered here since the 1920s, when the Salón Tenampa, still on the north side of the square, became the place to hear them. The square was remodelled after 2009, so older photos with the kiosk won't match what you see.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in front of Mercado San Camilito, beside the big GARIBALDI letters. The middle of the square is to the south of this spot, about 2 minutes on foot, so face south and let the letters, the maguey and the musicians fall into one view.

card.hook: Don't try to squeeze the whole Zócalo into one photo, because it's a 240 m by 240 m square and it will win. Pick one big building instead and let it be the star.
card.stand_here: Stand on the edge of the plaza in front of the Catedral Metropolitana's main facade, on the north side of the Zócalo, and face north so the facade fills your screen. The flagpole and the middle of the square will be behind you to the south.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole cathedral facade with some plaza in front. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved doors and tile patterns, or 0.5x if you want the facade plus a big sweep of open square.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the facade straight, then tap the facade and drag the slider a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out the carved stonework.
card.best_time: Check whether an event is setting up before you line up your shot, because stages and temporary arenas can block the view. If something is in the way, shift a few steps until you find a clear line, and take a few frames in case people walk through.
card.selfie_here: For a wide backdrop, try the terrace of the Gran Hotel Ciudad de México, next to the Zócalo, with the square spread out below you. Use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the plaza over your shoulder. It's more of a panorama than a close-up, so hold the phone a little further out. The rooftop of Círculo Mexicano, just behind the cathedral's dome, is another option. Both are reached through the hotel or restaurant.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand on the cathedral's western steps, up above the plaza, while you stand out in the square with the National Palace behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Cars drive around the Zócalo fast and sometimes run red lights, so watch the traffic when you cross. One review suggests arriving by subway instead. The cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Zoom in and get a shot of just the carved doors with nobody walking through, then see how long you can wait for the gap.
card.good_to_know: Long before the Spanish arrived, this was the heart of the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan, and the Templo Mayor site is just a block away. The cathedral was built in the latter half of the 16th century, and its three portals face south over the plaza. The name Zócalo means 'plinth': a column was planned as a monument to independence, but only the base was ever built.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the edge of the plaza in front of the Catedral Metropolitana's main facade, on the north side of the Zócalo, and face north so the facade fills your screen. The flagpole and the middle of the square will be behind you to the south.

card.hook: One slim pillar holds up a giant square concrete roof, and water pours around it like a curtain. It looks a bit like a magic trick, and it's the star of the museum's courtyard.
card.stand_here: Stand in the central courtyard, right under the canopy of El Paraguas ("the umbrella"), just inside the entrance. Face the column and take in the pool and the water falling around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole canopy, the column and the pool in one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to catch the carving on the column.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the column up with a vertical line so it stands straight, then keep a bit of pool and a few people at the bottom of the frame to show how big it all is.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon light is lovely for garden photos. The courtyard is inside the museum, so check the official site for current hours, and for whether the fountain is running, before you go.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in the central courtyard in front of the umbrella fountain, with the galleries behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and let the umbrella peek over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a full-building shot, ask someone to stand back just outside the main entrance on Paseo de la Reforma until the front of the building fills the frame, while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is not allowed, and selfie sticks aren't permitted (one traveller had theirs handed in at the entrance), so hold your phone with both hands and keep your elbows tucked in. Check the official site for tickets and photography rules.
card.challenge: Get the column perfectly straight on a gridline, with one stranger walking under the umbrella for scale. Bonus points if they don't notice they're famous now.
card.good_to_know: The National Museum of Anthropology is the largest and most visited museum in Mexico, with 3.7 million visitors in 2024. It opened in 1964 in Chapultepec Park, with 23 exhibition rooms built around this big courtyard. Outside, the gardens hold outdoor exhibits, including the Olmec colossal heads.

card.hook: Picture a pale marble palace with a golden dome, peeking out from behind a line of park trees. That's the Palacio de Bellas Artes, and the trees are the secret to making it look good.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Alameda Central, on the main east-west path at roughly the midpoint. Face east: the palace is straight ahead, with the dome behind a line of trees.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the trees, facade and dome all fit. Then try zoom 2x to bring the dome closer. Only use zoom 0.5x if you're right beside the building and can't step back.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white marble on the screen, then slide it a little darker so the facade keeps its detail instead of turning bright white.
card.best_time: Early morning, when the facade catches direct light.
card.selfie_here: Head to the front plaza by the main entrance, facing Av. Juárez, and put the building behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x to fit more of the palace in), and wait for a gap in the crowd so other tourists stay out of your shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the plaza slightly to the left of the path leading up to the building, so the whole facade fits in the frame, while you pose in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash photography is prohibited in most areas of the palace. It gets crowded, so keep an eye on your belongings and keep valuables safe.
card.challenge: Find the four Pegasus sculptures on the plaza side and get a close-up of one with the marble behind it.
card.good_to_know: Work began in 1904 under Italian architect Adamo Boari, but the heavy building sank into the soft ground and the Revolution halted construction in 1913. It was finished under Federico Mariscal and opened on 29 November 1934. It's sometimes called the "art cathedral of Mexico".

card.hook: Picture one long, dead-straight avenue running away from you, with the city skyline at the far end. That's the view from the castle terrace, and guides call it the classic postcard shot of Mexico City.
card.stand_here: Stand on the east terrace of Chapultepec Castle and face Paseo de la Reforma. The boulevard should run straight away from you towards the city centre.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole length of Reforma in one frame. Then try 1x for a tidier skyline, and 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the monuments in the traffic circles.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and run the boulevard along the middle line, then tap the boulevard and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning. Guides say afternoon light washes out the boulevard.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the east terrace, facing down Paseo de la Reforma, and arrive in the morning so the sun is behind you. Use the front camera and try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more of the view. For a second option, the Altar a la Patria monument in the park has the castle visible in the background of the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot upward from the foot of the hill beside the Niños Héroes monument, so the whole castle profile shows against the sky behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Entry to the terraces is through paid museum entry, so check the official site for current days, hours and ticket rules. Selfie sticks are listed as prohibited, and staff enforce this at the entrance. Phone photos are fine, but keep the flash off inside the museum. The castle sits on a steep hill with many stairs and uneven surfaces, and a shuttle train (with a fee) goes up the hill.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 5x and try to spot every monument in the traffic circles along Reforma. Bonus points if you can get one in the shot with your thumbs-up in the corner.
card.good_to_know: The castle sits on top of Chapultepec Hill, about 2,325 metres above sea level, and began in 1785 as a stately home for a Spanish viceroy. It later became a military academy, the home of Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlota, and a presidential residence. It has been the National Museum of History since 1939. Maximilian also ordered the straight boulevard that links the castle to the city centre, first called Paseo de la Emperatriz and now Paseo de la Reforma.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the east terrace of Chapultepec Castle and face Paseo de la Reforma. The boulevard should run straight away from you towards the city centre.

card.hook: Picture a 46-metre curve of shiny metal with no ordinary windows, and you've got the Museo Soumaya. It changes with the light, so it's one of those spots where your phone does most of the work.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza Carso, in the open plaza in front of the museum entrance. The museum is to the south-west of you, about 2 minutes on foot, so face south-west and step back until the whole building fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full facade. If you can't step back far enough, drop to 0.5x. Then go to 2x–5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with tiles.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright part of the facade, then slide it a little darker so the shiny tiles keep their detail and colour.
card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon, or the 30 minutes before sunset. The tiles on the facade you're facing turn a warm amber-gold.
card.selfie_here: Try the terrace of the Loma Linda restaurant in Plaza Carso, where a photo shows the museum in view behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and keep the building over your shoulder. It's a paid venue, so you may need to be a customer.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back in the open Plaza Carso and frame the whole museum facade with you in front of it.

card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: the whole curvy building, then a close-up of nothing but hexagons. Bonus points if the second one looks like abstract art.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: the best view of a 700-year-old temple comes with a menu. From the El Mayor terrace you look straight down on the Templo Mayor, with its stone layers stacked up like a very old cake.
card.stand_here: Stand on the El Mayor restaurant terrace at República de Argentina 15, on the corner of Justo Sierra. Face south-west, where the ruins lie below you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the whole excavated area in. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the platforms and sculptures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and put the ruins in the lower two-thirds of the frame, with a little of the Centro Histórico buildings for scale.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. The ruins have almost no shade, so it's much more comfortable than midday.
card.selfie_here: On the El Mayor terrace, use the front camera at 0.5x and tuck the Templo Mayor excavations in behind your shoulder. The rooftop cafeteria of the Porrúa bookstore on Justo Sierra also overlooks the site, and a photo guide praises its panoramic view.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by at the northeastern corner of the ruins to take your photo, so the cathedral shows up in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: The ruins are a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go. Photos without flash are allowed. The El Mayor terrace is a restaurant, so you're expected to order something.
card.challenge: Count how many layers of stonework you can spot from the terrace. Then try to find a serpent head up close once you're inside.
card.good_to_know: This was the main temple of the Mexica people in their capital, Tenōchtitlan, which is now Mexico City. It was dedicated to Huītzilōpōchtli, god of war, and Tlāloc, god of rain and agriculture. It was rebuilt six times, each stage over the one before. Full excavation began in 1978, after workers found a huge carved stone disk of the goddess Coyolxauhqui.

card.hook: A gold figure on top of a 36-metre column, with city traffic swirling round her feet. She looks great, but the trick is to step back and let the long, straight avenue do the framing.
card.stand_here: Use the crosswalks to reach the median strip (camellón) on the Chapultepec side of Paseo de la Reforma. Face east, with the Angel's column in front of you and the avenue stretching behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the column with the avenue running away behind it. Then try 2x to see how the modern towers sit beside the column. Use 0.5x only if you end up close and want the whole column in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and put the column on one of the vertical lines, so the avenue leads the eye straight to it.
card.best_time: Go on a Sunday morning, when Reforma is closed to cars and it's much easier to shoot. After dark, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows into your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the southwest corner of the roundabout (Glorieta del Ángel). A guide calls it the cleanest angle with the least traffic. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the golden column rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to wait at the crosswalk on the Chapultepec (west) side of the roundabout, then stand with the column behind you while they shoot back toward you.
card.rules_and_safety: The roundabout is busy, so cross only at crosswalks and when the lights allow it, and never step into the traffic lanes. Fencing or renovation boarding has been reported around the base, so close shots and the marble steps may be blocked.
card.challenge: Keep the gold Angel clear of the buildings behind her, so she stands out against the sky like she owns the place.
card.good_to_know: The Angel of Independence (officially the Monumento a la Independencia) was finished in 1910 for the centenary of the start of Mexico's War of Independence. The 6.7-metre bronze Nike on top is covered in 24k gold and was restored in 2006. A mausoleum for independence heroes lies beneath the column.

card.hook: Most people head for the classic east terrace at Chapultepec Castle. The south garden terrace is quieter and, many say, more atmospheric: a lake, a forest and, on a clear winter day, volcanoes on the horizon.
card.stand_here: Stand on the south garden terrace of Castillo de Chapultepec, right at the phone icon on the map (the castle grounds have paid entry). Face the park lake, with the volcanoes off to the southeast.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to get the terrace, lake and trees all in one frame, then try 1x for a more natural look. On a clear day, go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the volcanoes.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the lake on the lower third, then tap the lake and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Clear winter days are your best bet for seeing the volcanoes. Earlier in the day is often calmer on the terrace, but check the castle's opening times first.
card.selfie_here: On the castle terrace, use the front camera and turn so the building's architecture frames you from behind, with the forest in view. Want the castle in the background instead? Try standing in front of the Altar a la Patria monument.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the foot of the castle hill beside the Niños Héroes monument with the castle above you, and ask a passer-by to shoot upward.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't permitted inside the castle, and one older guide says to leave them at the second gate. Policies can change, so check on arrival. The castle grounds are ticketed, so check the official site for tickets and opening times.
card.challenge: Find a bit of balustrade or a leafy plant for the foreground, then see if you can get the lake, the forest and a volcano all in one shot.
card.good_to_know: Chapultepec means 'at the grasshopper hill' in Nahuatl, and Aztec rulers used the hill as a retreat. The castle on top was built in 1785 and later became home to Mexico's heads of state. It's also where the young cadets known as the Niños Héroes made their stand in 1847.

card.hook: You'll probably catch yourself walking backwards across the Zócalo, trying to fit this whole red palace in your screen. It runs for more than 200 metres, so it's a fair struggle.
card.stand_here: Stand on the west side of the Zócalo (Plaza de la Constitución) and face east. The palace is straight ahead, about 220 m away, roughly 3 minutes on foot across the open square.
card.zoom: Start at 1x with your phone held sideways to get the whole facade. Try 0.5x if you want more square and sky, or if people crowd the edges. Then go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the central balcony, the bell and the two towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal line, so the long facade doesn't tilt and the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when guides say the crowds are thinner. The facade may get more direct light later in the day, so if the sun is low behind the building, tap the palace and drag the slider to make the picture a bit darker, so the red stone keeps its colour.
card.selfie_here: Stand out on the open Zócalo with the palace facade behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it, so the long red front fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the square's northeast corner and shoot toward the palace, so the whole building fits in the frame with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The palace is a working government building and only some parts are open to visitors, so check the official site for interior access and photo rules. The Zócalo often hosts events, and a temporary ice rink has sometimes blocked the classic view.
card.challenge: Get both towers, the central balcony and a clear band of open square in one straight, level shot, with no tilt and no stranger's head.
card.good_to_know: The balcony above the central doorway is where the president gives the Grito on the evening of 15 September, just before 11pm, and rings the bell Father Miguel Hidalgo used to call for rebellion. The site has been a seat of power since the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II had his "New Houses" here, and some of that older building material was reused. Today it's also the president's official residence, with Diego Rivera's murals inside.

card.hook: Picture a 67 m stone arch with a copper dome, and kids splashing in fountains right in front of it. That's Plaza de la República, and it's a lot more fun than a normal monument stop.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de la República, across the plaza from the monument, with the fountains in front of you. Face west and you'll see the whole arch and its copper dome.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole arch with the fountains in front. Switch to 1x for a cleaner shot of just the monument, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the dome and stone sculptures.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the monument, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky stays blue and the stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the plaza. Check the sky first, because the dome and stone look best against blue or lightly clouded sky.
card.selfie_here: Head to the plaza side in front of the arch, beside the geyser-style fountains, and turn your back to the monument. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the arch fits behind you, and let the lively plaza fill in the rest.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the plaza facing the monument's front, with the fountains in the foreground, while you pose by the fountains so the whole arch fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza is an open public square. The observation deck is a paid entry, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on Live Photo and catch a splash of fountain water with the dome peeking out above it.
card.good_to_know: At 67 m, this is the tallest triumphal arch in the world. It began as a grand legislative palace under President Porfirio Díaz, with the first stone laid in 1910, but the Revolution stopped the work and the shell stood unfinished for about twenty-five years. It became a monument in the 1930s, was finished in 1938, and several key figures of the Revolution are buried inside.

card.hook: Picture a whole palace wearing blue-and-white Talavera tiles like a very fancy shirt, right in the middle of a busy pedestrian street. You can't really miss it, and honestly, why would you want to?
card.stand_here: Head for the pedestrian stretch of Avenida Francisco I. Madero and walk about 94 m north-east along it to reach the tiled facade at Madero 4. Stand on the street directly in front and face the building, so you can frame the whole front head-on.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole facade in from the street. If the pavement is narrow and the front won't fit, switch to 0.5x. Use 2x to zoom in on a patch of tiles or one of the balconies.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tiles, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the blue stays rich and the white doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go before 9am, when the light hits the tiles cleanly and the street is quieter. Midday light is flat, and the pavement gets crowded with people and vendors.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sidewalk outside the tiled facade at Madero 4 with the building behind you, since that's where visitors commonly pause for selfies. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the blue-and-white wall fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Walk along Madero to the corner with Filomeno Mata, where the blue-and-white house comes into view, and ask a passer-by to photograph you in front of the facade from there (check the spot on the ground, as crowds and layouts change).
card.rules_and_safety: The facade is fine to photograph from the public pedestrian street. The courtyard is a restaurant space, so check the official site for interior access and photo rules, and be considerate of the diners if you go in.

card.hook: Picture a big white curve of marble glowing against a wall of green trees, right in the middle of downtown Mexico City. That's the Hemiciclo a Juárez, and it's an easy photo win.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Hemiciclo a Juárez, southeast side, facing Avenida Juárez, on the south edge of Alameda Central. Look toward the monument so the white curve fills your view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the curve and lines look natural. If you're close and the whole curve won't fit, switch to 0.5x. For the fountain figure with the tower behind, try 2x to bring the tower closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the middle of the monument with the middle of the frame, with trees as a border on each side.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or at dusk, when the light is soft and the monument looks bright without harsh glare. At dusk, let night mode do its thing.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the Hemiciclo a Juárez, on the park's south side. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the big white monument in behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: If it's your first visit, go by day, since evenings call for more care. It's a public park, but check the official site before you go in case of works or temporary closures.
card.challenge: Once you've got the monument, wander into the park and find two more shots: a fountain lady with her pitcher and the Torre Latinoamericana behind her, and the Bellas Artes dome framed by trees down a path.
card.good_to_know: Alameda Central is the oldest public park in the Americas, laid out in 1592. The Hemiciclo honours Benito Juárez, one of Mexico's most beloved presidents. A 2012 renewal brought new marble paving and new trees, so the park looks fresh and bright.

card.hook: Tilt your phone up at the Torre Latinoamericana and just keep tilting. This slim steel tower came through the big 1985 quake without damage while buildings nearby were harmed, and it still looks calm about it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Torre Latinoamericana itself: the phone icon sits right in the middle of its outline, in downtown Mexico City. Face the tower from its base and shoot upwards, then step back across the street to fit the whole building in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower in from close up, then go to 1x for a natural look. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the upper floors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, because haze or cloud flattens the view. Late afternoon into dusk suits both the tower and the city lights, and night mode helps if you brace your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the pedestrian stretch of Francisco I. Madero street, where the tower rises at the far end of the avenue. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the tower over your shoulder. It's our suggestion rather than a known selfie spot, so check the exact spot on the map.
card.ask_someone: For a full-length shot, ask a passer-by to shoot from across the intersection in front of the Palacio de Bellas Artes, looking up at the tower from street level, and check the map first for the exact spot.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower is a working office building with a public observation deck on the 44th floor, so check the official site before you go for access and tickets. Up on the deck, press your phone close to the glass to cut reflections.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead straight on a gridline with a bit of street at the bottom, and no leaning allowed.
card.good_to_know: The Torre Latinoamericana is 166 m tall and opened on 30 April 1956. It was Mexico's tallest completed building for almost 27 years, until 1982. Many locals see it as a symbol of safety.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Torre Latinoamericana itself: the phone icon sits right in the middle of its outline, in downtown Mexico City. Face the tower from its base and shoot upwards, then step back across the street to fit the whole building in.

card.hook: This cathedral took just under 250 years to build, so it never quite picked one style, and that's what makes the stone front so fun to look at. The Zócalo gives you plenty of room to step back and fit all of it in.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Plaza de la Constitución, in the middle of the plaza, facing north toward the cathedral facade. You'll get the full stone front with both bell towers, the main entrance and the giant flag pole.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close or want the whole front plus some sky. From further back, zoom 1x looks more natural. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a bell tower or the carved portals.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines, holding your phone level so they don't lean.
card.best_time: Go early if you can. Morning light is warmer on the stone and there are fewer people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the tile patterns in front of the cathedral, on the square's north side, with the doors and stonework right behind you. Or stand by the big flagpole at the centre of the plaza and turn so the cathedral is behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the towers peek over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Madero Street facing the cathedral's front, and ask them to step back as far as the plaza allows so the full facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Outside photos are fine, but inside skip the flash and don't take photos during mass. Photography is restricted in the crypts. Drones are generally restricted in central Mexico City, including around the Zócalo. Events can close off or crowd the square, so check before you plan your shot.
card.challenge: Get both towers standing perfectly straight on the gridlines, with one tiny person in the foreground to show how huge the place is.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral was built between 1573 and 1813, so you'll spot Gothic, Baroque, Churrigueresque and Neoclassical styles in the stonework. It stands on the old Aztec sacred precinct, close to the Templo Mayor. It's about 59 metres wide and 67 metres to the tips of its two bell towers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Plaza de la Constitución, in the middle of the plaza, facing north toward the cathedral facade. You'll get the full stone front with both bell towers, the main entrance and the giant flag pole.

card.hook: There's a bronze huntress with water jets around her, right in the middle of one of Mexico City's biggest avenues. Start here and you get the classic Reforma shot without the Ángel crowds.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Fuente de la Diana Cazadora, about halfway along Paseo de la Reforma, using the pavements around the fountain. Face the Diana statue so her water jets sit in front of the wide avenue and its trees. From here, the old-centre end of the avenue lies to the north-east, about 2.3 km away in that direction.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the statue with the avenue and trees around her. Try 0.5x to fit in more avenue and tree canopy, or 2x (or higher, if your phone has it) for a tighter shot of the statue and her jets.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the statue on one of the lines, then tap her and slide the brightness down a little so the jets and sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the sculpture is lit. For fewer cars, aim for a Sunday morning, when the main downtown stretch is usually closed to traffic.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Diana fountain on its traffic circle, at the Reforma and Sevilla intersection. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the statue and the avenue fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For the Ángel instead, ask a passer-by to stand on the southwest corner of the Ángel de la Independencia roundabout and frame you in front of the monument so the whole thing fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic is heavy, so stay on the pavements and marked crossings, and wait for a gap before stepping into the road. Photography is generally fine in public spaces, but respect private property and any photo rules inside museums. Keep the phone strap on your wrist.
card.challenge: Can you catch the water jets and the whole statue in one shot, with the avenue's trees leading the eye behind her?
card.good_to_know: Reforma was laid out in the 1860s under Emperor Maximilian, who wanted a grand European-style boulevard linking the city centre with Chapultepec Castle. It was first named after his wife, Empress Carlota, and became Paseo de la Reforma in 1872. Today it's lined with hotels, offices and some of the city's tallest towers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Fuente de la Diana Cazadora, about halfway along Paseo de la Reforma, using the pavements around the fountain. card.hook: You're standing in a post office and you're about to say 'wow' out loud. Step into the main hall, look up, and watch the gold galleries stack away over your head.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of the ground-floor hall of the Palacio Postal, right where the phone icon sits, so there's no further walk once you're inside. Face straight ahead, then point your phone up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole atrium and all its galleries fit in one frame. Switch to 1x for the staircase and the ironwork details, and try 2x or 5x to pick out the ceiling (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap a mid-bright patch of the gold ironwork, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go when the building is open and the hall is quieter, so you get a clear view of the floor. Interiors can be dim, so hold your elbows against your body to keep steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the sprawling stairs in the main hall, which you reach through the north-side entrance for the Post Museum. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and let the stairs and gold trim fill the background. For a street selfie, stand on the front steps on Calle de Tacuba facing Bellas Artes, with the Postal Palace behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed inside, but skip the flash and follow any signs. Entry to the interior may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the galleries perfectly symmetrical on both sides, with the vertical lines dead straight, and then see if a friend can spot the one thing you tilted.
card.good_to_know: The atrium rises through stacked galleries of gilded ironwork under an ornate ceiling. From outside, the pale, ornate facade looks best from the corner of Eje Central Lázaro Cárdenas and Calle de Tacuba, which makes a nice opening shot before you go in.

card.hook: A bronze horse and rider are parked in front of a huge pale palace, and somehow they don't fight for attention. That's El Caballito and MUNAL, and one photo catches both.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza Manuel Tolsá, in front of the El Caballito statue, and face north toward the museum's main facade. The facade is only a short walk away, so you don't need to back up any further.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade and the statue together, then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look. For a close-up of the horse and rider or the facade details, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the building's edges straight, and if the pale stone looks washed out, tap the facade and slide a little darker.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the facade than the middle of the day.
card.selfie_here: Stay on Plaza Manuel Tolsá, out front, and turn so the Chiluca stone facade is behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your arm a little high so the building rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Calle de Tacuba end of the plaza while you stand across the plaza, so the full facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum doesn't allow selfie sticks, and photos inside must be taken without flash. Inside, photo sessions for personal or commercial use aren't authorized, and a separate photo permit is required, so check the official MUNAL page before you go. The plaza out front is often the scene of city protests, according to a museum guide.
card.challenge: Put El Caballito on the left or right of your frame so the museum's front door stays in view, then take a second, closer shot with the statue big and the facade soft behind it, like a postcard.
card.good_to_know: The building was designed by Italian architect Silvio Contri as the Palace of Communications, built to show Mexico's commitment to modernisation. It has been an art museum since 1982 and holds more than 3,000 works of Mexican art. The statue has stood in its present spot since 1979.

card.hook: The pin says "Centro Coyoacán", so you might expect a mall. The mall is gone, and the photo you want is in a leafy garden down the road with a bronze coyote fountain.
card.stand_here: Stand in Jardín Centenario, in front of the bronze Fuente de los Coyotes in the middle of the garden. The old mall site is to the north-west of it, about 1.3 km away. Face the fountain so the trees and arches wrap around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the fountain plus the trees and arches. If the fountain looks small or the crowd gets in the way, tap 0.5x. Use 2x for details of the Jardín Hidalgo kiosco from a distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain on the centre line, then tap the fountain and slide it a little darker so the bronze keeps its detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Early morning is lovely light and the least crowded. After dark the fountain is lit up, so use night mode and hold still for a second or two.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Fuente de los Coyotes in the middle of the park, with the arches of the former convent behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit more of the arches in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Avenida Francisco Sosa side of the old atrium gates, while you stand at the gates so they and the park frame you, with the church behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The Jardín Hidalgo kiosco may be under restoration, so scaffolding could hide it. Check before you go.
card.challenge: Get the fountain dead centre, an arch on each side, and not one stranger's elbow in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Guides name this the most photographed spot in Coyoacán. For a second picture, Jardín Hidalgo is just across the way, with its 19th-century kiosco, stained-glass cupola and bronze eagle, and the historic town hall behind. The Centro Coyoacán mall opened in 1989 as the first mall of El Palacio de Hierro, designed by Javier Sordo Madaleno. It closed on 19 September 2022, and its site is being absorbed into the neighbouring Mítikah complex.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Jardín Centenario, in front of the bronze Fuente de los Coyotes in the middle of the garden. The old mall site is to the north-west of it, about 1.3 km away. Face the fountain so the trees and arches wrap around it.
